Benchmarking quantum trial wavefunctions for phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo

Preprint: APS/123-QED

Abstract

The phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (ph-AFQMC) method is a stochastic imaginary-time projection technique for computing ground-state properties of strongly correlated quantum systems, with accuracy that depends critically on the choice of trial wavefunction. We present a comprehensive benchmarking study of trial wavefunctions prepared using parameterized quantum circuits, spanning unitary coupled cluster (UCC), Hamiltonian-informed, Jastrow-inspired, and adaptively constructed ansatzes, and evaluate their accuracy, expressibility, and resource requirements within the quantum-computing-enhanced AFQMC (QC-AFQMC) framework. Trial states are prepared with GPU-accelerated statevector simulations using CUDA-Q and tested on linear hydrogen chains under bond stretching and on nine closed-shell molecules at their equilibrium geometries with varying degrees of static correlation. We find that when ansatzes are compared at similar numbers of variational parameters, ph-AFQMC largely removes the differences between families for weakly and moderately correlated systems: for such molecules every trial yields a ph-AFQMC energy within chemical accuracy despite trial energy errors spanning nearly three orders of magnitude, whereas the choice of ansatz becomes consequential as static correlation grows. Our results indicate that the variational energy of a trial is not always a reliable indicator of its quality for ph-AFQMC, and reveal instances in which adding variational parameters can lower the trial energy while degrading the ph-AFQMC energy. Across all of our benchmark systems, trial fidelity ranks candidate trials more reliably than variational energy, and for spin-contaminated trials, the singlet-projected fidelity is more reliable than unprojected fidelity. The UCCSD ansatz initialized from unrestricted CCSD amplitudes provides a robust and inexpensive-to-optimize baseline across all benchmark systems, with circuit depth as its principal limitation, while adaptive and compact layered ansatzes remain competitive in accuracy in the strongly correlated regime with substantially shallower circuits. Finally, we find that UCCSD trial wavefunctions initialized from unrestricted rather than restricted Hartree–Fock references improve accuracy at stretched geometries but yield non-variational energies in the strongly stretched limit.

I Introduction

Determining the ground-state properties of interacting many-electron systems remains a central challenge in quantum chemistry, condensed matter physics, and materials science. Although the Schrödinger equation provides a complete description, in principle, its exact solution becomes intractable at even modest system sizes due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space. As a result, a variety of approximate methods have been developed to balance accuracy and computational cost. Methods such as Kohn–Sham density functional theory (DFT) and single-reference coupled cluster (CC) theory provide accurate descriptions for weakly correlated systems, but often fail in strongly correlated regimes where multi-reference effects become important. Here, we use strong (or static) correlation to refer to regimes in which no single Slater determinant (SD) provides a dominant description of the exact ground state [23].

Auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) has emerged as a highly accurate and scalable approach for treating strongly correlated systems [52, 67]. AFQMC achieves this by applying stochastic imaginary-time evolution to a population of single-SD walkers {|ϕ⟩}\{\ket{\phi}\}, which collectively project the many-body wavefunction toward the ground state. In its original formulation, referred to as free-projection (fp)-AFQMC [83], walkers evolve in SD space without any constraint, and fermionic antisymmetry leads to fluctuating walker signs/phases, resulting in the Monte Carlo sign/phase problem [71]. To mitigate this issue, constrained variants such as constrained path (cp-) [98] and phaseless (ph-) [99] AFQMC methods introduce a controllable bias through a trial wavefunction |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}}, where the overlaps, ⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi\rangle, guide the stochastic propagation of the walkers. In this work, we focus on the phaseless approximation, which has attracted significant interest and demonstrated considerable success in ab initio electronic structure calculations.

The ph-AFQMC method introduces a controllable approximation to the ground-state wavefunction, whose accuracy depends on the quality of the trial wavefunction |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}}, as reflected in its overlap with the true ground state and the phase constraint it provides [99]. In the simplest case, a single-SD mean-field solution such as spin-restricted (RHF) or spin-unrestricted Hartree–Fock (UHF) can be used as the trial. However, as systems become more strongly correlated, it becomes necessary to go beyond simple SDs and use linear combinations of determinants or multi-SD (MSD) wavefunctions. Most commonly, trial wavefunctions of this form can be constructed in various ways, such as through truncated [63, 18] or selected [24, 56] configuration interaction (CI), complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) [79], or non-orthogonal MSD approaches [49]. Throughout this work, “U” denotes unrestricted in UHF and unitary in acronyms for quantum ansatzes such as unitary coupled cluster (UCC).

More generally, classically constructing trial states that accurately capture many-body correlations remains a major challenge. The number of determinants in CI-like trial wavefunctions grows exponentially with system size, while truncating the expansion compromises size extensivity: the sum of the energies of non-interacting subsystems does not yield the same energy as treating the combined system. These limitations have motivated interest in trial states based on compact, nonlinear parameterizations of correlation, including Slater–Jastrow [55], matrix product state [38], and CC [46] forms, which encode correlations through the structure of the ansatz rather than through an explicit linear expansion over determinants. Recent work has also shown that perturbative CC trial wavefunctions can restore size extensivity in the subsequent ph-AFQMC calculation [100]. In practice, however, evaluating the overlaps and local quantities required by AFQMC with such correlated trial states can introduce substantial computational cost [96]. Quantum state preparation provides an alternative route to constructing correlated trial states within a systematically improvable circuit representation. Here, we investigate the utility of such quantum-prepared states as ph-AFQMC trials.

The quantum-computing-enhanced AFQMC (QC-AFQMC) approach was first introduced by Huggins et al. [36]. In this framework, the trial state is prepared on a quantum computer and subsequently used within ph-AFQMC simulations. In the original formulation, |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}} is prepared on a quantum device, and the classical shadows protocol [33] is employed to perform a series of randomized Clifford measurements that encode classical information about the quantum state. These measurement results are then used to estimate ⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi\rangle and ⟨ΨT|H^|ϕ⟩\langle\Psi_{T}|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle required during the ph-AFQMC simulation. It was subsequently shown that estimating the local energy, EL=⟨ΨT|H^|ϕ⟩⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩E_{L}=\frac{\langle\Psi_{T}|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi\rangle}, using classical shadows requires measurement data that scales exponentially with system size LL to maintain constant relative precision [60, 53]. This bottleneck arises because the amplitudes of correlated quantum trial states, |ΨT​(x)||\Psi_{T}(x)|, are typically exponentially small in system size (𝒪⁡(2−L)\mathcal{O}(2^{-L})). To overcome this bottleneck, a tomographic protocol tailored for fermionic systems, known as matchgate shadows, was later introduced [91]. Subsequent studies investigated the scaling behavior of QC-AFQMC with matchgate shadows and demonstrated that chemical accuracy could be achieved for small systems (<10<10 qubits), with a post-processing cost scaling polynomially as 𝒪⁡(N8.5)\mathcal{O}(N^{8.5}), where NN denotes the number of spin orbitals [32, 45]. More recently, a reduction in the computational cost to 𝒪⁡(N5.5)\mathcal{O}(N^{5.5}) through algorithmic optimizations and GPU-accelerated post-processing on a 16-qubit trial wavefunction has been reported [101]. This scaling is comparable to that of standard classical ph-AFQMC implementations [38], marking an important step towards making QC-AFQMC a practically viable hybrid quantum-classical algorithm. A complementary strategy is to bypass tomographic reconstruction altogether and evaluate the required trial-state overlaps explicitly. A related approach has recently been demonstrated for AFQMC using wavefunctions obtained from sample-based quantum diagonalization [21].

Despite substantial progress made in reducing the post-processing cost of QC-AFQMC, fundamental questions remain regarding the types of quantum trial states that are most effective in practice. Across various studies of QC-AFQMC to date, several forms of trial wavefunctions have been explored. While the original proposal used a simple non-variational valence-bond wavefunction and a hardware-efficient circuit [36], since then, the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) has been used to optimize trial wavefunctions for AFQMC constructed from well-established quantum chemistry ansatzes, including UCC with singles and doubles (UCCSD) [32, 3, 43], paired UCC with doubles (UpCCD) [101, 25], orbital-optimized UpCCD [25], as well as the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) [10] and the quantum number preserving ansatz [45], along with alternative QC-AFQMC formulations utilizing other trial states [44, 97]. Our work presents a comprehensive benchmarking study of a wide range of quantum trial ansatzes, including members of the UCC family, hardware-efficient, adaptive, and other variational forms.

We benchmark our ansatzes using linear hydrogen chains, which are widely regarded as an effective testbed for many-electron methods [64, 29, 35], and, as a second benchmark, we study nine closed-shell molecules at their equilibrium geometries. Despite their apparent simplicity, hydrogen chains exhibit a rich range of correlation effects. As the H–H bond length increases, the system transitions from a weakly correlated regime to a strongly correlated regime. At the same time, they avoid additional complexities present in heavier molecules and materials, such as the need to treat core electrons separately or include relativistic effects. Moreover, they provide a natural and systematic scaling with system size while preserving the essential correlation physics, enabling controlled studies of method performance as the Hilbert space grows. Hydrogen chains are, however, chemically homogeneous. To introduce greater chemical diversity, we use the molecular test set introduced in Section V. This set comprises first- and second-row hydrides and diatomics with single, double, and triple bonds, and ranges from weakly to strongly correlated at equilibrium geometry [68].

The quality of the trial states is assessed using several key metrics: the variational energy, the ph-AFQMC projected energy and its associated error, the ph-AFQMC accuracy as a function of the number of determinants, the unprojected and spin-projected fidelities with respect to the full configuration interaction (FCI) ground state, and the overall resource efficiency of optimizing and preparing the trial state.

Beyond characterizing the behavior and effectiveness of different trial wavefunctions within the QC-AFQMC framework, these results provide broader insight into the performance of modern VQE ansatzes at larger qubit counts under realistic computational constraints. Simulations were performed using GPU-accelerated quantum circuit simulations with CUDA-Q, NVIDIA’s open-source hybrid quantum–classical platform [87], with the workflow distributed across multiple compute nodes on the Perlmutter supercomputer. This enables scalable benchmarking of increasingly complex ansatzes and large-scale parallelization of trial-state optimization. Therefore, the present work complements existing VQE benchmarking studies [102] by examining these ansatzes in a hybrid quantum–classical setting leveraging high-performance computing resources. The trial wavefunctions analyzed here may also serve as correlated reference states or benchmarks for other many-body methods.

In addition to exploring various quantum ansatzes, we also explore different initial HF states that precede the variational circuit. While quantum circuits for VQE and QC-AFQMC for spin-symmetric molecules are typically initialized with the RHF state, we also investigate initialization from the UHF state. Under bond stretching and in strongly correlated regimes, UHF can yield spin-symmetry-broken solutions, providing a qualitatively improved description of static correlation. Although such states are spin contaminated and may have reduced overlap with the exact spin-symmetric ground state, previous AFQMC studies have shown that they can nevertheless improve performance and reduce phaseless bias, as the symmetry of the walker ensemble effectively enforces a symmetry-projected description [75, 51, 64, 2, 81]. More generally, symmetry-broken single SDs provide a simple and inexpensive means of capturing strong-correlation effects in AFQMC. Generalized Hartree–Fock (GHF) trials, which may break both SzS_{z} and S2S^{2} symmetries, have also been successfully applied to both molecular and lattice systems [76, 19, 15, 80], providing an important single-determinant baseline for comparison with more elaborate trial forms, including the quantum-prepared states studied here. Here, we examine how the choice of initial state influences AFQMC accuracy and stability across geometries.

The organization of the paper is as follows: in Sec. II we provide a summary of the various quantum ansatzes considered in this study; in Sec. III, we provide the main ingredients in the ph-AFQMC approach; in Sec. IV we provide the results of both VQE and AFQMC for the hydrogen chain under bond stretching, and compare RHF to UHF; in Sec. V, we test the transferability of these findings on a chemically diverse set of molecules at their equilibrium geometries; finally, we discuss our findings and draw conclusions in Sec. VI and Sec. VII.

II Trial wavefunctions for quantum chemistry

The second-quantized representation of the molecular Hamiltonian is:

H^=H^1+H^2=∑p​qNTp​q​ap†​aq+12​∑p​q​r​sNVp​q​r​s​ap†​aq†​as​ar,\hat{H}=\hat{H}_{1}+\hat{H}_{2}=\sum_{pq}^{N}T_{pq}a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{pqrs}^{N}V_{pqrs}a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}^{\dagger}a_{s}a_{r}, (1)

where NN denotes the number of basis functions in the chosen single-particle basis and ap†a_{p}^{\dagger}, aqa_{q} are fermionic creation and annihilation operators for orbitals indexed by p,qp,q.

Preparing accurate approximations to the ground state of H^\hat{H} is a central task in quantum algorithms for chemistry. The earliest quantum approaches to this problem were based on adiabatic state preparation and quantum phase estimation [22, 5, 1]. However, these methods require circuit depths that exceed the capabilities of current noisy quantum devices. Consequently, ground-state estimation on near-term hardware has shifted toward the VQE framework, which combines a parameterized quantum circuit with a classical optimizer. The quantum circuit prepares a compact variational trial state |Ψ⁡(𝜽)⟩=U⁡(𝜽)​|Φ0⟩|\Psi(\bm{\theta})\rangle=U(\bm{\theta})|\Phi_{0}\rangle for a given ansatz U⁡(𝜽)U(\bm{\theta}), while the parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} are iteratively updated to minimize the cost function, which is the expectation value of the Hamiltonian, ⟨Ψ⁡(𝜽)|H^|Ψ⁡(𝜽)⟩\langle\Psi(\bm{\theta})|\hat{H}|\Psi(\bm{\theta})\rangle. To estimate the energy of a trial state on a quantum computer, H^\hat{H} is typically mapped to a linear combination of Pauli operators using transformations such as the Jordan–Wigner (JW) [41] or Bravyi–Kitaev [11] mappings, after which the energy is computed as a weighted sum of Pauli expectation values.

For molecular systems described in a second-quantized representation, each qubit typically encodes the occupation of a spin orbital in the RHF basis used to construct H^\hat{H} in Eq. 1. The initial state of the variational circuit, |Φ0⟩\lvert\Phi_{0}\rangle, is therefore usually chosen as the RHF reference state |ΨRHF⟩\lvert\Psi_{\mathrm{RHF}}\rangle. However, we also explore initializing the circuit with the UHF reference state, i.e., setting |Φ0⟩=|ΨUHF⟩\lvert\Phi_{0}\rangle=\lvert\Psi_{\mathrm{UHF}}\rangle.

Optimizing the variational parameters that define the trial state, however, is complicated by barren plateaus. These are regimes in which the energy gradients with respect to circuit parameters vanish exponentially with system size [62], causing the cost landscape to become effectively flat and requiring an exponentially large number of measurements to resolve meaningful gradients and maintain desired precision, thus potentially eliminating any exponential advantage offered by variational quantum algorithms. To mitigate barren plateaus, two primary strategies have been proposed: the use of problem-inspired ansatzes and improved parameter initialization schemes [14]. Consequently, successful variational circuits in quantum chemistry are typically chemically inspired, with the UCC family of ansatzes serving as a prominent example [74]. The success of the UCC ansatz in VQE arises not only from its close correspondence to classical CC theory, but also from the fact that a significant portion of the correlation energy can be captured by initializing the variational parameters with second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation theory (MP2) [69, 78] or CCSD amplitudes [31]. It was shown in Ref. [31] that using CCSD amplitudes to initialize the UCCSD parameters consistently outperforms MP2-based initialization and can serve as good variational starting points even when CCSD returns non-physical energies. Other problem-inspired ansatzes were also explored in this work, including the Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz (HVA) [92, 72, 95], most commonly applied to lattice systems, and the unitary cluster Jastrow (UCJ) ansatz [59].

Due to hardware limitations, it is often necessary to explore informed truncations of these problem-inspired ansatzes. For instance, one can exploit molecular point-group symmetries to eliminate excitation operators in the UCCSD ansatz that do not preserve the symmetry of the Hartree–Fock reference state [12]. Other truncation methods include restricting the ansatz to kk repetitions of generalized and paired excitations, leading to the kk-UpCCGSD family of ansatzes [50]. Additionally, locality constraints can be imposed on the UCJ ansatz for hardware architectures with local qubit connectivity, resulting in the LUCJ form [66, 65]. Another prominent strategy is adaptive ansatz construction, as in the Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter VQE (ADAPT-VQE) algorithm, where operators from a predefined pool, such as those corresponding to UCCSD excitations, are iteratively selected and added based on their expected contribution to lowering the energy of the trial state [27].

These considerations motivate our selection of four representative families of quantum trial ansatzes. All four families have been executed on current hardware, at least in truncated form: UCCSD on trapped-ion and superconducting devices [30, 70, 28], paired UCC variants on trapped ions [102, 101], LUCJ on superconducting processors [66, 77], HVA for lattice models [82], and adaptive ansatzes via qubit-ADAPT [86, 7].

II.1 Unitary Coupled Cluster

The UCC ansatz is defined as an exponential of excitation operators acting on a reference determinant, which is usually the RHF state:

|ΨUCC⟩=eT^−T^†​|Φ0⟩,\ket{\Psi_{\text{UCC}}}=e^{\hat{T}-\hat{T}^{\dagger}}\ket{\Phi_{0}}, (2)

where T^\hat{T} is the excitation operator. In the standard UCC ansatz, excitations are allowed only from occupied to virtual molecular orbitals (MOs) of the reference state. In this case, when including up to nn-th order excitations, T^\hat{T} has the form:

T^=∑k=1nT^k,T^k=1(k!)2∑i,j,…occ∑a,b,…virθi​j​…a​b​…a^†aa^†b⋯a^ja^i,\hat{T}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\hat{T}_{k},\qquad\hat{T}_{k}=\frac{1}{(k!)^{2}}\sum_{i,j,\ldots}^{\text{occ}}\sum_{a,b,\ldots}^{\text{vir}}\theta_{ij\ldots}^{ab\ldots}\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{a}\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{b}\cdots\hat{a}_{j}\hat{a}_{i}, (3)

where occupied and virtual molecular orbitals are indexed by i,j,…i,j,\ldots and a,b,…a,b,\ldots, respectively. The variational parameters θi​j​…a​b​…\theta_{ij\ldots}^{ab\ldots} are associated with the corresponding excitation operators. To map the UCC ansatz to a quantum circuit, we first perform a Trotterization of the exponential operator. It has been shown that a single-step Trotter expansion can efficiently approximate the UCC ansatz [6, 16]. In this case, the factorized form of the ansatz can be written as:

|ΨUCC⟩=∏i,j,…occ∏a,b,…virexp⁡(θi​j​…a​b​…​G^i​j​…a​b​…)​|Φ0⟩,|\Psi_{\mathrm{UCC}}\rangle=\prod_{i,j,\ldots}^{\text{occ}}\prod_{a,b,\ldots}^{\text{vir}}\exp\!\left(\theta^{ab\ldots}_{ij\ldots}\hat{G}^{ab\ldots}_{ij\ldots}\right)|\Phi_{0}\rangle, (4)

where the anti-Hermitian generator G^i​j​…a​b​…\hat{G}^{ab\ldots}_{ij\ldots} is defined as a^i​j​…†a​b​…−a^a​b​…i​j​….\hat{a}^{\dagger ab\ldots}_{ij\ldots}-\hat{a}^{ij\ldots}_{ab\ldots}. By introducing a factor of ii to render G^\hat{G} Hermitian and mapping the resulting second-quantized operators to Pauli operators using the JW transformation, the UCC ansatz can be conveniently expressed on a quantum circuit as a product of exponentials of Pauli strings ei​θ​P^e^{i\theta\hat{P}}.

Most variants of the UCC ansatz modify Eq. (4) by restricting the allowed excitation operators. The letter labels in an ansatz name specify these constraints. For example, “S” and “D” correspond to single and double excitations, respectively. The label “G” denotes generalized excitations in which excitations are permitted between any molecular orbitals rather than being restricted to the occupied-to-virtual transitions of the reference determinant. Additionally, the label “p” indicates a paired ansatz, in which double excitations include only electrons in spin-paired units (i.e., (iα,iβ)→(aα,aβ)(i_{\alpha},i_{\beta})\rightarrow(a_{\alpha},a_{\beta})). Finally, a prefactor in the ansatz label (e.g., 3-UpCCGSD) denotes the number of circuit repetitions (layers), as is standard for compact paired ansatzes [50]. These constraints reduce the number of excitation operators and variational parameters, while still preserving expressivity.

II.2 Local Unitary Cluster Jastrow

The LUCJ ansatz is constructed by applying locality constraints on the more general UCJ ansatz. By combining chemically motivated structure with hardware-efficient locality, LUCJ aims to provide a low-depth, yet expressive, alternative to UCC.

The general kk-layer UCJ ansatz has the form:

|ΨUCJ⟩=∏l=0k−1𝒰^l​ei​𝒥^l​𝒰^l†​|Φ0⟩,|\Psi_{\text{UCJ}}\rangle=\prod_{l=0}^{k-1}\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{l}\,e^{i\hat{\mathcal{J}}_{l}}\,\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{l}^{\dagger}|\Phi_{0}\rangle, (5)

where each 𝒰^l\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{l} is a particle-number-conserving orbital rotation operator, and each 𝒥^l\hat{\mathcal{J}}_{l} is a diagonal Coulomb operator of the form:

𝒥^l=12​∑i​j,σ​τJi​j,lσ​τ​n^i,σ​n^j,τ,\hat{\mathcal{J}}_{l}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij,\sigma\tau}J^{\sigma\tau}_{ij,l}\,\hat{n}_{i,\sigma}\hat{n}_{j,\tau}, (6)

where n^i,σ=ai,σ†​ai,σ\hat{n}_{i,\sigma}=a^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}a_{i,\sigma} is the fermionic number operator. Orbital rotations can be decomposed into nearest-neighbor Givens rotations [93, 39], enabling efficient implementation on qubit architectures with limited connectivity. In the spin-balanced case, the Jastrow operator 𝒥^l\hat{\mathcal{J}}_{l} is fully characterized by two symmetric matrices: Jα​α=Jβ​βJ^{\alpha\alpha}=J^{\beta\beta}, which couple same-spin orbitals, and Jα​β=Jβ​αJ^{\alpha\beta}=J^{\beta\alpha}, which couple opposite-spin orbitals. The non-zero entries of these matrices determine which spin orbitals (and hence qubits) are coupled.

To impose locality, we mask out all interactions except those between nearest neighbors in the chosen qubit layout. In our simulations, we assume a simple square topology in which the α\alpha and β\beta qubits occupy two parallel rows adjacent to one another. Under this layout, the following coupling patterns implement strictly nearest-neighbor interactions:

Jα​α\displaystyle J^{\alpha\alpha} :{(p,p+1),p=0,…,N−2},\displaystyle:\{(p,p+1),\quad p=0,\ldots,N-2\}, (7)
Jα​β\displaystyle J^{\alpha\beta} :{(p,p),p=0,…,N−1},\displaystyle:\{(p,p),\quad p=0,\ldots,N-1\},

where NN denotes the number of MOs. Thus, kk-LUCJ is obtained by masking 𝒥^\hat{\mathcal{J}} in Eq. (5) according to a locally constrained coupling map, such as the one defined in Eq. (7).

The variational parameters of the LUCJ ansatz are the non-zero matrix elements of the corresponding orbital-rotation matrix of operator 𝒰^l\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{l} and the corresponding Jastrow matrices of operator 𝒥^l\hat{\mathcal{J}}_{l}. Analogous to the UCCSD ansatz, the LUCJ ansatz can be initialized using CCSD tt-amplitudes by applying a double factorization of the T2T_{2} operator to approximate the UCJ form [66]:

eT^2−T^2†=ei​∑l=0k−1𝒰^l​𝒥^l​𝒰^l†≈∏l=0k−1𝒰^l​ei​𝒥^l​𝒰^l†,e^{\hat{T}_{2}-\hat{T}_{2}^{\dagger}}=e^{\,i\sum_{l=0}^{k-1}\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{l}\hat{\mathcal{J}}_{l}\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{l}^{\dagger}}\;\approx\;\prod_{l=0}^{k-1}\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{l}\,e^{i\hat{\mathcal{J}}_{l}}\,\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{l}^{\dagger}, (8)

where the final expression follows from a first-order Trotter approximation. However, enforcing locality by masking out non-nearest-neighbor interactions can significantly degrade the quality of this factorization. To mitigate this effect, one may employ a compressed double factorization with appropriate regularization [54, 85].

II.3 ADAPT-VQE

The ADAPT-VQE algorithm [27] constructs the ansatz dynamically during optimization. This algorithm begins with a reference state |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle and a Hamiltonian H^\hat{H}, as in standard VQE for molecular systems, but rather than specifying a fixed ansatz, ADAPT-VQE grows the circuit by selecting operators from a predefined operator pool. In our work, this pool consists of the UCCSD excitation operators, referred to as ADAPT-UCCSD.

At the beginning of each ADAPT iteration nn, the energy gradient with respect to each operator A^j\hat{A}_{j} in the pool is evaluated:

∂E(n)∂θj=⟨ψ(n)|[H^,A^j]|ψ(n)⟩,\frac{\partial E^{(n)}}{\partial\theta_{j}}=\left\langle\psi^{(n)}\middle|\left[\hat{H},\hat{A}_{j}\right]\middle|\psi^{(n)}\right\rangle, (9)

where |ψ(n)⟩|\psi^{(n)}\rangle is the state produced by the current ansatz.

After computing all gradients, the operator with the largest gradient magnitude, corresponding to the steepest expected reduction in energy, is appended to the ansatz together with a new variational parameter. All parameters, including the newly added one, are then re-optimized to obtain the next state |ψ(n+1)⟩|\psi^{(n+1)}\rangle.

This cycle of gradient evaluation, operator selection, and parameter re-optimization is repeated until a convergence criterion is satisfied, typically when all gradient magnitudes fall below a specified threshold or when successive energy changes become smaller than a given tolerance. ADAPT-VQE therefore constructs a compact, chemically inspired ansatz that often yields significantly shallower circuits than fixed-structure UCC ansatzes, at the cost of computing energy gradients with respect to the entire operator pool at each iteration. In practical implementations on quantum hardware, this cost is further compounded by the need to estimate these energy gradients from finite-shot measurements. However, this additional sampling overhead may be more manageable than the circuit depth requirements associated with less compact ansatzes [27].

II.4 Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz

The HVA is motivated by the idea that the structure of the many-body Hamiltonian itself should guide the design of the variational circuit. Rather than employing an excitation-based ansatz, the HVA constructs the variational state using unitary evolutions generated directly by Hamiltonian terms. This approach is inspired by adiabatic state preparation and Trotterized time evolution, in which sequential evolution under non-commuting Hamiltonian components drives the system toward low-energy states.

After applying the JW transformation, we decompose the resulting qubit Hamiltonian as:

H^=∑p=0P−1H^p,\hat{H}=\sum_{p=0}^{P-1}\hat{H}_{p}, (10)

where each term H^p\hat{H}_{p} consists of a sum of mutually commuting Pauli operators, and different terms do not commute, [H^p,H^p′]≠0[\hat{H}_{p},\hat{H}_{p^{\prime}}]\neq 0 for p≠p′p\neq p^{\prime}. Because the Pauli operators within a given H^p\hat{H}_{p} commute, the corresponding unitary evolution, exp⁡(−i​θ​H^p)\exp(-i\theta\hat{H}_{p}), can be implemented exactly as a product of Pauli rotations, without introducing any Trotter approximation error.

A kk-layer HVA (labeled as kk-HVA) is defined as a layered product of such unitary evolutions:

|ΨHVA⟩=∏l=0k−1∏p=0P−1e−i​θp,l​H^p​|Φ0⟩,\ket{\Psi_{\text{HVA}}}=\prod_{l=0}^{k-1}\prod_{p=0}^{P-1}e^{-i\theta_{p,l}\hat{H}_{p}}|\Phi_{0}\rangle, (11)

where θp,l\theta_{p,l} are the variational parameters, and once again |Φ0⟩=|ΨRHF⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle=|\Psi_{\text{RHF}}\rangle. The HVA layers act as a controlled mechanism for systematically entangling and correlating the RHF state in directions dictated by the physical Hamiltonian.

This ansatz can be interpreted as a variationally optimized form of Trotterized time evolution, in which the effective evolution times associated with each Hamiltonian term are treated as independent variational parameters. As the number of layers increases, the expressive power of the HVA systematically improves. In the limit of large depth, the ansatz approaches a variationally optimized Trotterized time evolution and can approximate the ground state of many local Hamiltonians [92].

III ph-AFQMC Overview

In AFQMC, as in other projector QMC methods, we approximate the exact ground state, |Ψ0⟩\ket{\Psi_{0}}, via imaginary time evolution:

|Ψ0⟩=limτ→∞e−τ​H^​|ΦI⟩.\ket{\Psi_{0}}=\lim_{\tau\rightarrow\infty}e^{-\tau\hat{H}}\ket{\Phi_{I}}. (12)

This expression is formally exact provided that ⟨ΦI|Ψ0⟩≠0\langle\Phi_{I}|\Psi_{0}\rangle\neq 0. Numerically, the continuous imaginary-time evolution is implemented through a discrete-time iteration, |Ψ(n+1)⟩=e−Δ​τ​H^​|Ψ(n)⟩\ket{\Psi^{(n+1)}}=e^{-\Delta\tau\hat{H}}\ket{\Psi^{(n)}}, where Δ​τ\Delta\tau is a small imaginary-time step.

In our QC-AFQMC simulations, we prepare |ΨT⟩|\Psi_{T}\rangle by running GPU-accelerated VQE with a chosen quantum ansatz, extracting the optimized statevector, and expanding it into an MSD wavefunction of the form:

|ΨT⟩=∑n=1Ndetscn​|Dn⟩.\ket{\Psi_{T}}=\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{dets}}}c_{n}\ket{D_{n}}. (13)

Given a set of NN MOs, typically obtained from an RHF mean-field solution, each |Dn⟩\ket{D_{n}} denotes a determinant corresponding to a specific occupation configuration of MM electrons distributed among NN spatial orbitals per spin (i.e., NN α\alpha and NN β\beta orbitals). Once the trial state is expressed in MSD form, the remainder of the workflow reduces to standard classical ph-AFQMC.

The specific QMC variant depends on how the imaginary-time evolution is implemented, i.e., the space used to represent the wavefunction and the importance sampling employed to control the fermionic sign/phase problem. In AFQMC, an arbitrary state at imaginary time τ\tau, |Ψ⁡(τ)⟩\ket{\Psi(\tau)}, is represented by a weighted ensemble of single-SD walkers {|ϕ⁡(τ)⟩}\{\ket{\phi(\tau)}\}. Each walker is expressed in terms of spin-resolved orbital-coefficient matrices Φα∈ℂN×Mα\Phi^{\alpha}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times M_{\alpha}} and Φβ∈ℂN×Mβ\Phi^{\beta}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times M_{\beta}}, corresponding to the occupied spin orbitals for the α\alpha and β\beta spin sectors, respectively.

The population of walkers, each initialized in the RHF occupation, explores the manifold of SDs through the application of one-body propagators of the form B^=exp⁡(∑i​ja^i†​Ui​j​a^j)\hat{B}=\exp\!\left(\sum_{ij}\hat{a}_{i}^{\dagger}U_{ij}\hat{a}_{j}\right), which, by Thouless’ theorem, generate new SDs via orbital transformations induced by the one-body propagator. Consequently, to perform imaginary-time propagation while preserving the single-SD structure of the walkers, the two-body interaction H^2\hat{H}_{2} must be recast in terms of one-body operators. In AFQMC, this is achieved through a combination of a Trotter–Suzuki decomposition of the imaginary-time propagator, a factorization of the two-electron integrals (e.g., via Cholesky decomposition), and a Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation that introduces auxiliary fields. These steps transform the two-body propagator into a stochastic average over one-body propagators parameterized by a set of auxiliary fields.

As a result, the imaginary-time propagator can be written in the compact form:

e−Δ​τ​H^=∫dNaux​𝐱​p​(𝐱)​B^​(𝐱)+𝒪⁡(Δ​τ2),e^{-\Delta\tau\hat{H}}=\int d^{N_{\mathrm{aux}}}\mathbf{x}\,p(\mathbf{x})\,\hat{B}(\mathbf{x})+\mathcal{O}(\Delta\tau^{2}), (14)

where p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}) is a normalized Gaussian distribution and B^​(𝐱)\hat{B}(\mathbf{x}) is a one-body propagator depending on the sampled auxiliary fields 𝐱\mathbf{x}. This integral is evaluated stochastically by sampling the auxiliary fields and propagating each walker with the corresponding one-body propagator. A detailed derivation of this procedure is provided in Appendix B.

As already discussed, if no constraint were introduced, we would have effectively implemented fp-AFQMC. Propagation would be highly noise-prone due to the fermionic phase problem that worsens with increasing imaginary time τ\tau and system size. To control this instability, Zhang and Krakauer introduced the phaseless approximation [99], described in detail in Appendix B. In this formulation, propagation is guided by a trial wavefunction |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}} through importance sampling. The overlap between each walker and the trial state, ⟨ΨT|ϕ⟩\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi\rangle, enters the importance-sampling transformation that steers the random walk toward regions of Slater-determinant space where overlap with the trial state has large magnitude. At each imaginary-time step, the auxiliary-field sampling distribution p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}) is shifted by an optimal force bias derived from this overlap, while the walker weights are updated according to the resulting importance function.

In addition, the phaseless constraint suppresses uncontrolled phase rotations by projecting the walker weights onto the real axis defined by the phase of the trial wavefunction. This procedure stabilizes the simulation while introducing a controllable bias whose magnitude depends on the quality of |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}}. In particular, the trial wavefunction defines the reference phase against which the stochastic propagation is constrained, so the phaseless bias depends on how closely the phase structure of |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}} matches that of the true ground state. Because the exact phase structure of the ground state is not known in advance, identifying optimal trial wavefunctions for ph-AFQMC remains a nontrivial problem.

IV Benchmark Results: Hydrogen Chains

To benchmark our quantum trial wavefunctions, we perform exact statevector simulations using optimized circuits with GPU accelerators. We implement all ansatzes using CUDA-Q [87] and perform ideal multi-node, multi-GPU statevector simulations. This enables efficient evaluation of our quantum circuits, provides exact statevector representations of the trial states, and allows seamless integration with our AFQMC pipeline. All quantum circuit simulations were run on NVIDIA A100 GPUs on the Perlmutter supercomputer at NERSC. We parallelize the wavefunction optimization by distributing gradient evaluations, whether with respect to variational parameters or operator pool elements, across multiple GPUs and compute nodes.

As previously mentioned, each resulting statevector is expanded into an MSD trial wavefunction of the form given in Eq. 13, which is then passed directly to the AFQMC calculation. Detailed descriptions of ansatz implementations, wavefunction optimization procedure, AFQMC hyperparameters, and the associated statistical analysis are provided in Appendix A.

We first use the STO-6G basis on a family of linear hydrogen chains under bond stretching. In this minimal basis, an NN-atom chain corresponds to NN spatial orbitals (and thus 2​N2N qubits), enabling controlled tests of our ansatz families as the system size increases. Near equilibrium geometries (R≈1.0​ÅR\approx 1.0~\text{\AA}), the electronic structure is dominated by dynamic correlation, and single-reference methods such as RHF and CCSD provide a qualitatively reasonable description of the ground state. In this regime, quantum ansatzes that closely resemble single-reference CC forms, such as UCCSD, perform competitively as both VQE solvers and as AFQMC trial wavefunctions. At stretched bond lengths (R≳1.2​ÅR\gtrsim 1.2~\text{\AA}), the system develops strong multi-reference character, with both static and dynamic correlation becoming significant. Here, conventional single-reference approaches like CCSD and MP2 begin to break down when built on a spin-restricted reference. CCSD based on an unrestricted determinant often remains qualitatively correct at stretched geometries, at the cost of spin contamination [48]. The CCSD amplitudes used to initialize our ansatzes are unrestricted for this reason (Appendix A). This regime is particularly challenging and serves as a critical test for more expressive ansatz families, as well as for the ability of AFQMC to recover correlation energy when supplied with quantum MSD trial wavefunctions. This makes the strongly stretched regime particularly well suited for assessing the robustness of quantum-derived trial states in AFQMC.

IV.1 VQE Results

Since the UpCCGSD, LUCJ, and HVA ansatzes are relatively compact in their single-layer forms, they are most commonly employed in a multilayer construction, where their expressivity can be systematically enhanced with increasing depth. Consequently, we consider both a single layer (k=1k=1) and a depth kk chosen such that the total number of variational parameters is approximately equal to that of UCCSD. This parameter-matching procedure enables a more direct comparison at roughly fixed expressivity. We note that the parameter kk is not directly commensurate across different ansatz families, as a single layer corresponds to distinct circuit structures and parameter counts in each case. In our plots and tables, the selected depth is prepended to the ansatz label (e.g., 7-HVA). Resource requirements for all ansatz families, including circuit depth scaling, parameter counts, and number of optimization iterations, are summarized in Table 1 and Table 2. All VQE evaluations for H10\mathrm{H}_{10} were parallelized across 16 compute nodes totaling 64 GPUs. For a comprehensive study of the effect of increasing the number of layers for these multi-layer ansatzes on H8, see Figure 8 in Appendix D.

Figure 1(a) presents the VQE energy errors in the potential energy surface (PES) for the symmetric stretch of the H10\mathrm{H}_{10} chain (20 qubits), across 7 bond lengths spanning from weakly to strongly correlated regimes. The absolute energy error |EVQE−EFCI||E_{\mathrm{VQE}}-E_{\mathrm{FCI}}| is reported on a logarithmic scale and includes the RHF error as a reference for the onset of strong correlation. Figure 1(b) shows the corresponding ph-AFQMC errors obtained from the same states, and is discussed in Section IV.2. Figure 2 complements this analysis by showing the fidelity |⟨ΨVQE|ΨFCI⟩|2|\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{VQE}}|\Psi_{\mathrm{FCI}}\rangle|^{2} between the optimized VQE states and the exact ground state obtained from FCI. These fidelities, along with the corresponding ⟨S^2⟩\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle values, are summarized in Table 2.

Across all bond lengths, UCCSD remains the most consistent and reliable ansatz overall, serving as the natural reference standard throughout this study. It achieves among the lowest energy errors at every geometry and maintains among the highest fidelities across the dissociation curve. Its strong and stable behavior is further aided by initialization with CCSD amplitudes, which significantly reduces the optimization cost relative to the other ansatzes.

ADAPT-UCCSD remains a close second to UCCSD in both energy and fidelity across the entire PES. Its key advantage is circuit compactness, especially at large bond lengths where the number of selected operators decreases as correlation increases.

The LUCJ and 3-LUCJ equilibrium accuracies are modest compared to UCCSD, but the LUCJ curves remain nearly flat across increasing correlation and 3-LUCJ even outperforms UCCSD in total energy error in the strongly correlated regime (R≳1.4​ÅR\gtrsim 1.4~\text{\AA}). Here, LUCJ achieves comparable accuracy with a significantly shallower circuit and requires only nearest-neighbor two-qubit gates. Its fidelity with the ground state also degrades more gently than those of the other low-depth alternatives. However, the lower overlap at larger bond lengths contrasts with its improved energy error, indicating a significant overlap with the low-lying spectrum of the Hamiltonian, but not necessarily the ground state. This indicates that judging the quality of the ansatz based on energy alone might be misleading.

Although single-layer HVA underperforms relative to the other ansatzes, it exhibits consistent and systematic improvement as the number of layers is increased. At sufficient depth (e.g., 7-HVA), HVA closely approaches the accuracy of UCCSD across all bond lengths.

UpCCGSD underperforms relative to the other ansatzes across all bond lengths considered. Increasing the number of layers does not lead to consistent or systematic improvements in the energy, and both the single-layer and multilayer variants yield the highest VQE energy errors and lowest fidelities among the ansatzes studied.

Regarding optimization behavior, UCCSD was the most straightforward ansatz to train, largely due to the effectiveness of CCSD-based parameter initialization. In contrast, UpCCGSD was the most challenging ansatz to optimize. CCSD warm starts were less consistently beneficial, particularly for multilayer circuits, likely because the generalized operator pool introduces many additional excitation operators with vanishing CCSD amplitudes. Moreover, all-zero initialization occasionally resulted in premature convergence to suboptimal local minima. These optimization difficulties also made it hard to obtain systematic improvements by simply increasing the number of layers. Although ADAPT-UCCSD is expressive, compact, and flexible, these benefits come at the cost of expensive optimization, as the algorithm iteratively selects and re-optimizes operators. This results in a substantially larger number of energy evaluations during the optimization process than for the other methods considered, making it the most resource-demanding ansatz in our study. LUCJ was also comparatively resource-intensive to optimize, with iteration counts often exceeding those of the other ansatzes. Prior work has noted that quasi-Newton methods such as L-BFGS-B can struggle for this ansatz, and that stochastic reconfiguration or linear-method optimizers can substantially improve convergence [65]. We did not encounter major optimization issues for HVA during our hydrogen chain experiments, and its performance improved systematically with additional layers; nonetheless, standard HVA can exhibit barren plateaus, which can be mitigated through principled initialization schemes [72]. We did not employ these more advanced optimization or initialization strategies in order to maintain a fair and consistent comparison across all ansatzes. More generally, the VQE energy landscape is non-convex and a local optimizer guarantees only a local minimum [9, 4, 94]. All trial states reported here should therefore be understood as the outcome of a fixed, reproducible optimization protocol rather than as certified global minima. Global-search strategies such as genetic algorithms [17, 90] could reduce this uncertainty at considerably higher cost and are left for future work.

IV.2 AFQMC Results

We employ these optimized quantum states as trial wavefunctions for AFQMC and compare their performance, as well as the simplest classical trial wavefunction, the RHF state. A comparison of the two panels of Figure 1, together with the fidelities in Figure 2, shows that standard variational diagnostics, including VQE energy and state fidelity, are not perfect predictors of AFQMC performance. In particular, although UCCSD yields among the lowest VQE energies across the geometries, the deepest HVA circuit (7-HVA) produces the most accurate AFQMC energies despite having a higher variational energy. This highlights that variational optimality alone is not a sufficient indicator of trial quality for ph-AFQMC.

Fidelity provides a more reliable qualitative guide. ansatzes with higher fidelities generally produce more accurate AFQMC energies, and the ranking of ansatz families by fidelity in Figure 2 broadly mirrors their AFQMC performance. In particular, 7-HVA achieves among the highest fidelity trials and the most accurate projected energies. However, this relationship is not strictly monotonic. For example, the UpCCGSD ansatz exhibits relatively poor fidelity but yields moderately accurate AFQMC energies at larger bond lengths. To understand this behavior, we consider the role of spin symmetry. UpCCGSD exhibits significant spin contamination (Table 2); however, because the Hamiltonian is spin symmetric and the walkers are initialized in RHF states, the walker ensemble remains in the correct spin sector, even when the trial wavefunction breaks this symmetry. As a result, AFQMC effectively samples a state closer to the spin-projected trial wavefunction.

This observation motivates a modified diagnostic. Since Sz=0S_{z}=0 throughout, we project the trial state onto the singlet subspace using the exact polynomial projector

P^S=0=∏s=1Smax(I−S^2s⁡(s+1)),Smax=Nα+Nβ2,\hat{P}_{S=0}=\prod_{s=1}^{S_{\max}}\left(I-\frac{\hat{S}^{2}}{s(s+1)}\right),\qquad S_{\max}=\frac{N_{\alpha}+N_{\beta}}{2}, (15)

in which each factor annihilates the component of total spin S=sS=s while leaving the singlet component unchanged. The normalized singlet-projected state is |ΨS=0⟩=P^S=0​|ΨT⟩/⟨ΨT|P^S=0|ΨT⟩|\Psi_{S=0}\rangle=\hat{P}_{S=0}|\Psi_{T}\rangle/\sqrt{\langle\Psi_{T}|\hat{P}_{S=0}|\Psi_{T}\rangle}, and we define the spin-projected fidelity as

FS=0=|⟨ΨFCI|ΨS=0⟩|2.F_{S=0}=\left|\langle\Psi_{\mathrm{FCI}}|\Psi_{S=0}\rangle\right|^{2}. (16)

By construction FS=0≥FF_{S=0}\geq F, with the gap growing with the degree of spin contamination. Figure 2 shows both quantities on the same axes: open markers denote the spin-projected fidelities for points where spin projection produces an appreciable change. Because the walker ensemble is restricted to the spin-symmetric manifold, we therefore expect and observe FS=0F_{S=0} to provide a more informative measure of trial quality whenever the ansatz breaks spin symmetry. We return to this point in Section V, where we quantify how well each diagnostic predicts ph-AFQMC accuracy across the full benchmark set.

A key distinction among ansatzes is the smoothness and stability of the projected energy curves. The AFQMC energies obtained from UCCSD, ADAPT-UCCSD, 3-LUCJ, and 7-HVA trials are smooth and nearly indistinguishable across the potential energy surface, suggesting that sufficiently expressive ansatzes capture the phase structure relevant for the phaseless constraint. In contrast, the UpCCGSD trials produce visible cusps and irregular behavior in the strongly correlated regime. This behavior may reflect the more difficult optimization landscape, where convergence to different local minima at adjacent geometries can produce trial states with inconsistent phase structure along the PES. For comparison, the single-determinant RHF trial, despite having poor fidelity and variational energy, yields a smooth AFQMC curve that simply deviates systematically from the exact result.

Taken together, these observations suggest that the effectiveness of a trial wavefunction in ph-AFQMC is governed less by variational optimality and more by the accuracy and stability of its phase structure. ansatzes, such as UCCSD, ADAPT-UCCSD, LUCJ, and HVA appear to capture this structure consistently once sufficient expressivity is reached, resulting in smooth and nearly identical AFQMC energy curves, whereas optimization difficulties in UpCCGSD lead to inconsistencies in the resulting phase structure. We report our VQE and AFQMC results for each ansatz at representative bond lengths R=1.0,1.4,and​ 1.8​ÅR=1.0,1.4,\ \text{and}\ 1.8~\text{\AA} in Table 2, providing numerical values corresponding to the data shown in Figures 1 and 2. The table also includes analogous results for H8, for which we observe that relative trends in energies and fidelities are consistent with those of H10, indicating that our findings generalize across system size in hydrogen chains.

In Figure 3, we present the AFQMC energy errors as a function of the number of determinants in each trial wavefunction. These results were obtained by truncating the full multi-determinant expansion, keeping the determinants with the largest coefficients, and renormalizing the truncated state. As expected, increasing the bond length enhances the multi-reference character of the system and, consequently, a larger number of determinants is required for the AFQMC energies to plateau. Also, increasing the number of determinants systematically improves the AFQMC accuracy in all cases. Overall, the different ansatzes exhibit qualitatively similar behavior as the number of determinants increases, and the observed differences appear to stem primarily from intrinsic trial quality rather than from a fundamentally more compact representation of correlation. In other words, no particular ansatz systematically captures significantly more correlation with fewer determinants than the others. Nevertheless, for all ansatzes considered, relatively compact approximations to the full trial wavefunction are sufficient to achieve converged AFQMC energies, especially near equilibrium geometries. This observation is particularly important in practice, as the trial overlap computation, which depends on the number of determinants, is the primary computational bottleneck of AFQMC. We note that these determinant-truncation results depend on the choice of single-particle basis. All results in Figure 3 are obtained in the canonical RHF MO basis, whereas alternative choices, such as localized orbitals or natural orbitals obtained from a correlated wavefunction, can substantially alter the compactness of the MSD expansion and therefore the number of determinants required to reach converged ph-AFQMC energies [34].

In Figure 4, we focus specifically on the ADAPT-UCCSD trial by extracting the wavefunction after every ten iterations of the ADAPT-VQE algorithm and using each as a trial wavefunction for AFQMC. By construction, ADAPT-VQE monotonically lowers the variational energy as additional operators are appended to the ansatz until convergence. Consequently, as the number of operators increases in Figure 4, the trial energies decrease strictly monotonically. As expected, we observe a general trend of improving AFQMC accuracy as the number of operators increases, followed by a plateau once the projected energy saturates. However, this improvement is not strictly monotonic. At the intermediate bond length (R=1.4R=1.4 Å), after reaching its optimal AFQMC accuracy, the continued addition of operators leads to a gradual increase in AFQMC energy error, indicating ADAPT-VQE may over-optimize directions irrelevant (or harmful) for AFQMC.

This behavior does not appear to be solely attributable to statistical fluctuations and instead reflects a distortion in the phase structure of the trial wavefunction. We also note that the statistical uncertainty of the AFQMC simulations decreases as we increase the number of operators. This result indicates that systematic improvements in trial variational energy do not necessarily translate into improved AFQMC performance, further emphasizing the nontrivial relationship between variational optimality and the phase structure relevant to the phaseless constraint. This observation is consistent with similar recent findings that lower variational energies do not necessarily lead to more accurate ph-AFQMC energies [20, 3].

We also compare the AFQMC energies obtained from ADAPT-VQE trials to the corresponding AFQMC(UCCSD) results, shown as horizontal reference lines. This comparison reveals the operator count at which the adaptive trial surpasses the full UCCSD trial in AFQMC accuracy. Notably, although the UCCSD ansatz for H10 contains 875 operators (Table 2), in the strongly correlated regime a substantially smaller, adaptively selected subset of operators is sufficient to achieve superior AFQMC accuracy. This highlights the practical advantage of adaptive ansatz construction in generating compact yet high-quality AFQMC trial wavefunctions.

IV.3 UHF Initialization

We have performed a brief study comparing RHF- and UHF-based trials, the results of which are shown in Figure 5. Our implementation of AFQMC(UHF) trials follows the protocol of the Simons Foundation hydrogen chain benchmarking study [64]. As a validation step, we first reproduce the reported energies for the corresponding geometries; our results are summarized in Table 5 and show excellent agreement.

AFQMC(RHF) and AFQMC(UHF) simulations for our set of geometries are performed using a projection time of τ=200​EHa−1\tau=200\,E_{\text{Ha}}^{-1}. To obtain stable UHF solutions at stretched geometries, we explicitly break the spin symmetry of an RHF initial guess during the self-consistent field procedure to prevent convergence back to the restricted solution. As expected, the RHF and UHF mean-field solutions begin to diverge near R≈1.0R\approx 1.0 Å, signaling the onset of static correlation, with UHF capturing additional correlation energy beyond this point.

We next report VQE energies obtained with the UCCSD ansatz initialized with reference states |ΨRHF⟩\ket{\Psi_{\mathrm{RHF}}} and |ΨUHF⟩\ket{\Psi_{\mathrm{UHF}}}, labeled UCCSD-RHF and UCCSD-UHF, respectively, with all variational parameters initialized to zero. We focus on UCCSD in this study because it is a widely used benchmark ansatz for VQE, allowing the effect of the reference state to be isolated while holding the variational form fixed. The circuits for the two initializations have the same variational structure; the difference arises from optimizing with respect to either the original Hamiltonian in the RHF spin-orbital basis or the classically rotated Hamiltonian in the UHF spin-orbital basis. Equivalently, this change of orbital basis can be represented in the original RHF basis by applying the corresponding fermionic orbital rotation to the UHF-based state. The resulting VQE energies are nearly identical at near-equilibrium bond lengths and begin to deviate slightly around R=1.6R=1.6 Å, where correlation effects become more pronounced.

These optimized trial states are then supplied to AFQMC. For the UHF-initialized circuits, the statevector is classically rotated back to the original RHF orbital basis before AFQMC is performed. As shown in Figure 5, AFQMC(UCCSD-RHF) and AFQMC(UCCSD-UHF) yield nearly identical results near equilibrium, but begin to diverge around R=1.6R=1.6 Å. In the intermediate stretched regime, the UHF-initialized trial produces systematically lower AFQMC errors, indicating improved phaseless constraint quality due to the enhanced static-correlation character of the UHF reference. At larger bond lengths (R≳1.8R\gtrsim 1.8 Å), we observe non-variational AFQMC energies (i.e., E<EFCIE<E_{\mathrm{FCI}}). This behavior can be expected, as ph-AFQMC is not a strictly variational method [13, 51, 57]. Similar trends are observed when comparing single-determinant AFQMC(UHF) and AFQMC(RHF): UHF-based trials improve accuracy in the bond-stretched regime but can also introduce non-variational energies in the strongly stretched limit.

V Benchmark Results: Molecular Test Set

Hydrogen chains isolate the crossover from dynamic to static correlation in a single, cleanly parameterized coordinate, but they are chemically homogeneous. To test whether the conclusions of Section IV transfer, we repeat the benchmark on nine closed-shell molecules at their experimental equilibrium geometries: BeH2, BH3, CH4, NH3, H2O, N2, C2, Be2, and C2H2. All calculations again use the STO-6G basis, so that FCI reference energies remain accessible, and the quantum calculations correspond to 14–20 qubits. For all systems except C2H2, both VQE state preparation and ph-AFQMC are performed in the full orbital space. For C2H2, the two carbon 1​s1s orbitals are frozen during quantum state preparation, yielding a CAS(10e,10o) trial, which is subsequently embedded into the full orbital space for the ph-AFQMC calculation. The reported C2H2 VQE energy error is measured relative to the full-space FCI energy and therefore includes the 0.70 mHa by which the CASCI(10e,10o) energy lies above the full-space FCI energy, i.e., the core-correlation energy that no active-space ansatz can recover, whereas the trial fidelity is evaluated relative to the corresponding CASCI ground state. All reported ph-AFQMC energies are obtained in the full orbital space. For each molecule the five ansatzes are compared at matched parameter counts, with the repetition count kk of the multilayer ansatzes chosen per system to approximate the UCCSD parameter count. Unlike the hydrogen-chain calculations, for which each trial was obtained from a single optimization with deterministic initialization, ansatzes in the molecular benchmark exhibited greater sensitivity to initialization and were therefore optimized from multiple Gaussian-perturbed starting points, as detailed in Appendix A. Full numerical results are collected in Table 3.

To place these systems on a common footing with the hydrogen chains we use the weight of the RHF determinant in the exact ground state, wHF=|⟨ΦRHF|ΨFCI⟩|2w_{\mathrm{HF}}=|\langle\Phi_{\mathrm{RHF}}|\Psi_{\mathrm{FCI}}\rangle|^{2}, as a simple proxy of multireference character: wHF→1w_{\mathrm{HF}}\rightarrow 1 for a perfect single reference, and it falls as static correlation grows. Values for every system studied here are tabulated in Table 4. The molecular set spans wHF=0.97w_{\mathrm{HF}}=0.97 (H2O) down to 0.660.66 (C2), and therefore interleaves with the hydrogen-chain series rather than duplicating it: the weakly correlated hydrides fill in the region above wHF=0.95w_{\mathrm{HF}}=0.95 that H10 never reaches, while Be2 (0.770.77) and C2 (0.660.66) provide strong static correlation at equilibrium geometries. Taken together the two benchmarks cover wHFw_{\mathrm{HF}} from 0.970.97 down to 0.140.14 across sixteen systems.

Figure 6 summarizes the results. The comparison between the two panels is the central observation. At the VQE level the ansatzes remain widely separated on every molecule as the errors span 0.100.10–76.776.7 mHa, and only UCCSD and ADAPT-UCCSD are consistently around the boundary of chemical accuracy, with UpCCGSD the worst performer on most of the systems. After ph-AFQMC projection this spread largely collapses. For the seven weakly and moderately correlated molecules (wHF≥0.85w_{\mathrm{HF}}\geq 0.85) every trial, including the UpCCGSD states whose variational errors exceed 20 mHa, yields a projected energy within chemical accuracy; the largest error anywhere in that group is 1.51.5 mHa. The choice of ansatz, which matters a great deal variationally, is almost irrelevant to the final projected energy. Only for Be2 and C2, the two strongly correlated members of the set, does the ansatz choice reassert itself. For these two molecules, just 30% of the trials reach chemical accuracy and the errors span 0.430.43–10.810.8 mHa. This reproduces, in a chemically diverse setting, the pattern seen along the H10 curve, where the ansatzes are nearly indistinguishable near equilibrium and separate only under bond stretching.

The relative standing of the ansatz families is broadly consistent with the hydrogen-chain results, with one notable exception. UCCSD and ADAPT-UCCSD are again the most reliable, and ADAPT-UCCSD attains comparable accuracy with far fewer parameters, confirming that adaptive construction yields compact trials across chemically diverse systems and not only for hydrogen chains. LUCJ similarly retains the favorable tradeoff observed for H10, providing competitive ph-AFQMC accuracy with a substantially shallower, locality-constrained circuit (Table E). HVA, however, does not transfer as successfully. Although 7-HVA was among the most accurate trials along the H10 dissociation curve, it is never cleaeryl the best-performing trial in the molecular test set and gives the largest ph-AFQMC errors for C2.

The clearest molecular illustration of the spin-symmetry argument developed in Section IV is provided by C2. The UpCCGSD trial for this molecule is heavily spin contaminated, ⟨S^2⟩=0.66\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle=0.66, and has by far the lowest raw fidelity of the five, F=0.652F=0.652 against 0.8940.894 for HVA. Raw fidelity would therefore rank it last. In fact its projected energy, +3.2+3.2 mHa, is markedly better than that of HVA, +10.8+10.8 mHa. The spin-projected fidelities resolve the discrepancy: FS=0=0.932F_{S=0}=0.932 for UpCCGSD against 0.9070.907 for HVA, an ordering that matches the ph-AFQMC result. This is the same effect identified for stretched H10, now observed at an equilibrium geometry of a genuine molecule, and it is the only system in the molecular set where the two fidelity measures differ appreciably, consistent with the fact that the remaining trials are nearly spin pure.

Combining the two benchmarks allows the relative predictive value of these diagnostics to be compared quantitatively. Figure 7 measures, for each of the sixteen systems studied, how often the ordering of a pair of trials according to a given diagnostic agrees with their ordering by absolute ph-AFQMC error. We quantify this agreement using pairwise concordance. For each system, we consider all (52)=10\binom{5}{2}=10 pairs of parameter-matched trials and ask whether the diagnostic correctly identifies which trial has the smaller ph-AFQMC error. The concordance is then simply the fraction of trial pairs that are ordered correctly, C=Nconcordant/NpairsC=N_{\mathrm{concordant}}/{N_{\mathrm{pairs}}}, where Npairs=10N_{\mathrm{pairs}}=10 for each system. Thus, C=1C=1 indicates that the diagnostic correctly ranks every pair of trials, C=0C=0 that it ranks every pair incorrectly, and C=0.5C=0.5 is the value expected from random ordering. No ties occur in our data. In this case, the concordance is directly related to Kendall’s rank correlation coefficient [42] by C=(1+τ)/2C=(1+\tau)/2. We base our conclusions on the consistency of the ordering across all sixteen systems rather than on any individual system. An uncertainty-aware version of this analysis, restricted to trial pairs whose ph-AFQMC energies are statistically resolvable and with bootstrap confidence intervals over systems, is given in Section F and yields the same ordering of the three diagnostics.

Three features stand out. Firstly, across the systems considered here, spin-projected fidelity is never less concordant with ph-AFQMC accuracy than unprojected fidelity, which in turn is never less concordant than variational energy; FS=0F_{S=0} is strictly more concordant than FF in five systems, while FF is strictly more concordant than variational energy in four. Secondly, for the first half of the systems, which are weakly and moderately correlated systems, the three diagnostics generally give the same ordering, with a median concordance of 80%. In this regime, essentially all trials already yield ph-AFQMC energies within chemical accuracy, limiting the practical significance of differences among their rankings. Thirdly, the diagnostics separate as the multireference character increases, with median concordances of 60%, 70%, and 90% for variational energy, FF, and FS=0F_{S=0}, respectively, among the strongly correlated systems. In the stretched hydrogen chains, the concordance of variational energy eventually falls to the random-ordering baseline, whereas FS=0F_{S=0} remains at 90% through R=1.8R=1.8 Å.

The improvement of FS=0F_{S=0} over FF is concentrated in a relatively small number of spin-contaminated trials, primarily UpCCGSD in the stretched hydrogen chains and C2. Spin projection should therefore be viewed as a correction that becomes important when spin symmetry is broken rather than as providing a uniform improvement across all trials. Moreover, at the most stretched geometry considered, H10 at R=2.0R=2.0 Å, the concordance of all three diagnostics decreases substantially. Across the present benchmark, fidelity therefore provides a more reliable ranking diagnostic than variational energy, particularly when spin contamination is accounted for, but it is not a universal predictor of phaseless bias, consistent with recent reports that higher trial fidelity need not translate into improved ph-AFQMC energies [46, 47].

VI Discussion

Our VQE results on H10 show that UCCSD remains the most consistent and reliable, general-purpose ansatz across the entire potential energy surface, benefiting substantially from chemically informed parameter initialization. In particular, CCSD warm-starts significantly reduced optimization difficulty and yielded strong variational energies and fidelities at weak-to-moderate correlation. ADAPT-UCCSD closely tracks UCCSD in both energy and fidelity while producing systematically more compact circuits in the strongly correlated regime. LUCJ exhibits comparatively modest equilibrium accuracy, but its error remains nearly constant across bond lengths, demonstrating robustness to increasing correlation. Additionally, the multilayer form (3-LUCJ) becomes competitive with UCCSD in the strongly correlated regime while requiring only nearest-neighbor two-qubit connectivity under the assumed square-topology qubit layout. HVA shows the most systematic depth-driven improvement: although single-layer HVA underperforms, at sufficient depth (e.g., 7-HVA) it approaches the accuracy of UCCSD. UpCCGSD proves the most challenging ansatz to optimize and generally underperforms across the geometries considered, with multilayer variants not yielding consistent improvement. These VQE trends are consistent with the broader observation that chemically structured ansatzes and informed initialization strategies can substantially improve optimization behavior at higher qubit counts, while more compact ansatzes may require careful depth selection and specialized optimization techniques.

When these optimized states are then used as trials to ph-AFQMC, several central conclusions emerge. Notably, the relationship between VQE optimality and AFQMC performance is nontrivial: trial variational energy alone is not a reliable predictor of ph-AFQMC accuracy. In contrast, fidelity with respect to the FCI ground state generally provides a more informative qualitative indicator of AFQMC performance, particularly away from extreme bond lengths. When the optimized trial exhibits appreciable spin contamination, as observed for several UpCCGSD and HVA trials, the relevant quantity is the fidelity of the singlet-projected trial, since that is the component the spin-restricted walker ensemble samples; across all sixteen systems it ranks candidate trials at least as reliably as the raw fidelity, which in turn is at least as reliable as the variational energy (Section V). This reinforces the key point that the effectiveness of a trial in ph-AFQMC depends not only on variational optimality or unprojected fidelity but also on the phase structure that enters the phaseless constraint.

We observe that increasing ansatz expressivity generally improves the quality of the phase structure relevant for ph-AFQMC. Across LUCJ, HVA, and UpCCGSD, moving from single-layer to parameter-matched multilayer constructions typically yields smoother projected-energy behavior and reduced AFQMC error. Importantly, under approximately fixed parameter budgets, multiple ansatz families produce comparable AFQMC performance, but the strength of this statement depends on how strongly correlated the system is. For the weakly and moderately correlated molecules of Section V it is clear, as every ansatz, including those with variational errors above 20 mHa, delivers a projected energy within chemical accuracy, so the ansatz choice is effectively immaterial and the cheapest adequate circuit should be preferred. In the strongly correlated regime the families separate clearly, by an order of magnitude on C2 and across the stretched hydrogen chains, and the choice of ansatz once again matters. The practical reading is therefore conditional: sufficient expressivity is what matters, and near equilibrium the bar for “sufficient” is low enough that most ansatzes clear it. This observation is consistent with our determinant-truncation analysis, where all trial families exhibited qualitatively similar convergence of AFQMC energies with the number of retained determinants. Differences between methods therefore largely reflect intrinsic trial quality rather than a systematically more compact MSD representation.

Despite these broad similarities, clear tradeoffs among ansatzes emerge. HVA achieves the strongest overall ph-AFQMC performance in our H10 study, including cases where it does not yield the lowest VQE energy, further underscoring that AFQMC accuracy depends on more than variational optimality. This advantage does not, however, transfer to the chemically diverse molecular test set, where HVA is never clearly the best trial and gives among the largest ph-AFQMC errors for the two most strongly correlated molecules, Be2 and C2 (Section V). This system dependence is consistent with the construction of HVA, which is particularly natural for structured lattice Hamiltonians, such as Hubbard- and Heisenberg-type models, that decompose into a small number of physically meaningful local terms. Molecular electronic-structure Hamiltonians mapped to qubits instead contain a much larger and less local collection of Pauli terms, making the direct HVA construction considerably less compact. In the implementation considered here, where every Pauli term is exponentiated once per layer, the uncompiled two-qubit gate count exceeds that of UCCSD by roughly a factor of five for H10 and four for C2, and that of LUCJ by more than two orders of magnitude (Table 6). The classical optimization runtime cost of HVA is also substantial, exceeding that of the cheapest ansatz for C2 by more than a factor of twenty (Table 6). Thus, while HVA can provide highly accurate ph-AFQMC trials for the regular hydrogen-chain problem, its accuracy does not transfer as consistently to the broader molecular benchmark and comes with unfavorable resource costs for molecular Hamiltonians.

LUCJ offers a compelling alternative: it is compact, locality-constrained, and naturally compatible with hardware connectivity, while remaining competitive in ph-AFQMC when given sufficient depth. UCCSD remains a robust baseline with strong and consistent results, particularly when paired with unrestricted CCSD warm-starts, although its gate-depth scaling and operator count become limiting for larger systems. In contrast, UpCCGSD, while compact, exhibits significant optimization difficulties; its ph-AFQMC curves are less smooth and in some cases display unpredictable behavior, including instances of non-variational projected energies. This highlights the practical risk of using ansatzes whose optimization landscapes are difficult to navigate. Although analogous optimization and approximation issues can arise in constructing classical MSD trials, variational quantum circuits introduce circuit trainability as an additional consideration: the quality of the resulting phaseless constraint depends not only on the states that the ansatz can represent in principle, but also on whether those states can be reliably reached through circuit optimization.

Finally, ADAPT-UCCSD combines strong performance with compactness. Our analysis in Figure 4 reveals that the best ph-AFQMC performance is often achieved before full ADAPT convergence, suggesting a promising strategy for producing high-quality, resource-efficient trials by terminating the adaptive procedure once the projected energy saturates.

We also examined the effect of the mean-field reference used to initialize the quantum trial using UCCSD along the H10 bond-stretching curve. Consistent with prior AFQMC studies, UHF-based references become advantageous in the intermediate stretched regime, where symmetry breaking provides a qualitatively improved description of static correlation and can improve AFQMC accuracy. At the same time, in the strongly stretched limit, we observe occasional non-variational behavior, which emphasizes that UHF-based trials can be beneficial but must be applied judiciously. Our findings are consistent with similar reports that unrestricted trials have led to non-variational energies [20]. The use of a UHF reference is not limited to UCCSD and is, in principle, compatible with the other ansatzes considered here. For LUCJ we primarily employ the spin-balanced formulation, in which Jα​α=Jβ​βJ^{\alpha\alpha}=J^{\beta\beta}, but this restriction can be relaxed to obtain a spin-unbalanced variant. In that case, one could use a UHF reference state and apply the corresponding orbital rotation to the Hamiltonian in the same manner as done for UCCSD. Similarly, for the HVA, the Pauli operators may be constructed from the Hamiltonian expressed in the UHF-rotated basis. The sensitivity to UHF initialization may depend on the structure and expressivity of the ansatz [8, 88], and a systematic investigation of this dependence across different circuit families is left for future work.

Since all simulations in this work are performed in the noiseless setting, corresponding to ideal statevector-based implementations of the trial wavefunctions, our comparisons are most directly relevant to fault-tolerant quantum computing, where deep circuits and precise state preparation are feasible. Notably, prior quantum hardware implementations of QC-AFQMC have demonstrated a degree of inherent noise resilience [36, 32, 101]. Nevertheless, the relative performance of different ansatz families may be affected in the presence of noise, particularly for deeper or more highly entangled circuits. Despite this, many of the qualitative trends observed here, such as the reduced sensitivity of ph-AFQMC to variational energy accuracy and the comparable performance of different ansatz families at matched parameter counts, are expected to persist, as they primarily reflect properties of the AFQMC-projected state obtained via imaginary-time propagation rather than the specific details of the underlying circuit implementation. Understanding the interplay between noise, ansatz structure, and AFQMC performance remains an important direction for future work.

VII Conclusion

In this work, we present a comprehensive benchmarking study of quantum trial wavefunctions for ph-AFQMC within the QC-AFQMC framework. Building on recent algorithmic progress that has brought the post-processing cost of matchgate-shadow QC-AFQMC close to the scaling of classical AFQMC, our focus was on a complementary and fundamental question: which families of quantum trial states provide the most effective phaseless constraints in practice, and what tradeoffs arise among expressivity, optimization cost, circuit depth, and AFQMC performance? To address this, we benchmarked a broad set of chemically and physically motivated ansatzes, including members of the UCC family (UCCSD and UpCCGSD), LUCJ, HVA, and adaptive constructions such as the ADAPT-VQE algorithm based on the UCCSD operator pool. Using GPU-accelerated statevector simulations distributed across multiple nodes, we optimized each ansatz via VQE, expanded the resulting statevector into an MSD trial wavefunction, and then performed standard classical ph-AFQMC using these trials. Linear hydrogen chains in a minimal STO-6G basis under bond stretching were selected as a controlled benchmark, along with a second benchmark of nine closed-shell molecules at their equilibrium geometries with varying degrees of static correlation. Our results demonstrate that quantum-generated trial states can provide reliable constraints for ph-AFQMC as several ansatz families achieve chemical accuracy near equilibrium geometries, while the most expressive trials remain close to this threshold even in the strongly correlated regime. From an alternative perspective, ph-AFQMC may be viewed as an effective classical post-processing step for quantum ground-state estimation [21].

This work provides several practical guidelines for QC-AFQMC trial design. Several of the trends identified here have analogues in the classical AFQMC literature. Our results establish how these principles manifest for quantum-prepared trials, for which trial quality is additionally shaped by the structure and symmetry properties of the variational circuit, its trainability, and the quantum and classical resources required for state preparation. The guidelines below therefore encompass both general principles of ph-AFQMC trial quality and the additional design tradeoffs introduced by quantum state preparation.

(i) Trial variational energy alone is not a reliable metric for phaseless performance; diagnostics that better capture wavefunction quality, such as fidelity or symmetry-projected fidelity in small systems or scalable measures of state similarity, are more informative. Quantifying this across all sixteen systems studied, spin-projected fidelity is never less concordant with ph-AFQMC accuracy than unprojected fidelity, which in turn is never less concordant than variational energy when the diagnostics are used to rank candidate trials for a given system. The three separate most clearly in the strongly correlated regime, where trial choice is most consequential. When a trial breaks spin symmetry, the singlet-projected fidelity provides the more relevant diagnostic because the spin-restricted walker ensemble means that ph-AFQMC effectively samples the projected component of the trial.

(ii) UCCSD initialized from unrestricted CCSD amplitudes provides a strong and reliable baseline for molecular QC-AFQMC trials.
