Across both benchmark sets it yields consistently accurate ph-AFQMC energies, while the physically informed warm start makes the variational optimization comparatively inexpensive, even for the strongly correlated systems considered here. Its principal limitation is circuit depth: the number of excitation operators and resulting gate count grow rapidly with system size. Thus, when circuit depth is not the dominant constraint, warm-started UCCSD provides a useful default against which more compact or hardware-oriented trial constructions can be assessed.

(iii) Increasing the number of variational parameters, and thereby enhancing expressivity, generally improves phaseless performance across ansatzes provided that the enlarged parameter space remains tractable to optimize. When parameter budgets are approximately matched, different ansatz families exhibit comparable AFQMC behavior for weakly and moderately correlated systems. Differences among ansatzes become more pronounced as static correlation increases, emphasizing the need to consider trial properties beyond variational energy, including information about symmetries and, where available, measures of state similarity.

(iv) Hardware-aware constructions, such as LUCJ, can remain competitive in ph-AFQMC while offering substantial advantages in circuit depth and connectivity. On the two most strongly correlated systems studied, LUCJ yields substantially shallower circuits than the other ansatzes considered (Table 6), giving the most favorable accuracy–gate-count tradeoff observed here.

(v) Adaptive ansatzes offer a practical path to compact, high-quality trials, and early stopping based on AFQMC-relevant saturation criteria may substantially reduce quantum resources. ADAPT-UCCSD yields the shortest circuit of the UCC family, with an uncompiled two-qubit gate count approximately an order of magnitude below that of UCCSD, but this compactness comes at additional classical cost because operator-pool gradient screening must be performed before each operator is appended (Table E). Where circuit depth is the binding constraint this can represent a favorable exchange, whereas the advantage is less clear when classical optimization cost is the dominant limitation.

(vi) Orbital choices and symmetry breaking can provide an additional axis for improving trials in strongly correlated and bond-stretched molecules without increasing quantum resources.

(vii) Conclusions drawn from a single family of systems should be treated with caution. HVA, which performs particularly well for the highly regular hydrogen chains, does not retain the same advantage across the chemically diverse molecular test set, illustrating the importance of benchmarking trial constructions across systems with different correlation and electronic-structure characteristics.

Several directions follow naturally from this study. A systematic exploration of orbital optimization and spin-unbalanced generalizations across various ansatzes could clarify when symmetry breaking is beneficial and how it should be combined with variational circuit structure to minimize phaseless bias. More scalable trial-quality diagnostics that correlate directly with phaseless performance would enable principled early-stopping criteria and more efficient trial selection at larger system sizes where fidelities are unavailable. Extending these benchmarks beyond minimal basis sets, to larger active spaces and to systems such as transition-metal complexes and lattice models, remains important for establishing how far the present conclusions reach; the restriction to STO-6G here is set by the need for exact FCI references against which the phaseless bias can be measured. A systematic study of the single-particle basis, and of ansatzes built on symmetry-broken references such as GHF, are further natural extensions. As QC-AFQMC continues to mature algorithmically and experimentally, the results presented here help map the practical design of quantum trial wavefunctions and highlight concrete strategies for balancing expressivity, hardware constraints, and ph-AFQMC accuracy in realistic hybrid quantum–classical workflows.

Data and Software Availability

The complete implementation used in this work, encompassing GPU-accelerated VQE and ph-AFQMC simulations with quantum trial wavefunctions, is publicly available at: https://github.com/rr637/QC-AFQMC.

Appendix A Simulation Details

All Hamiltonian integrals, SCF, CCSD, and FCI calculations were performed using the PySCF [84] quantum chemistry package. wave function parameters were optimized with the L-BFGS-B optimizer from the SciPy library [89], using an energy tolerance of 10−610^{-6} Ha. For ADAPT-VQE, we used a gradient magnitude convergence threshold of 10−310^{-3}. Gradients were estimated using central finite-difference methods with a parameter shift of ϵ=10−3\epsilon=10^{-3}. The OpenFermion package [61] was used to construct UCC excitation operators, while the ffsim library [85] was used to generate the matrix representations required for the LUCJ ansatz, which were then decomposed into quantum gates.

Our UCCSD and UpCCGSD ansatzes were constructed using non–spin-adapted and non–spin-complemented excitation operators. Consequently, the ansatzes are built from spin-orbital excitations that conserve the spin projection SzS_{z}, but do not explicitly enforce total spin symmetry, as excitation operators are assigned independent variational parameters. We use warm-start initialization of these parameters with unrestricted CCSD t1t_{1} and t2t_{2} values. In cases where CCSD did not converge (e.g., for R≳1.8​ÅR\gtrsim 1.8\,\text{\AA} in H10), we initialized all variational parameters to zero so that the initial circuit reduces to the identity acting on |Ψ0⟩\lvert\Psi_{0}\rangle. The ordering of operators in the UCCSD ansatz is not uniquely defined [26, 27]. Following Ref. [31], we therefore employ magnitude ordering, in which operators are ordered according to the absolute values of their initial CCSD parameters |θ||\theta|, with operators having larger magnitudes placed to the right in Eq. 4 of the main text to reduce Trotter error. Operators with zero initial CCSD parameter values, such as generalized excitation operators, were placed at the end of the ansatz and ordered lexicographically by spin-orbital indices. We found that multilayer UpCCGSD was difficult to optimize when all variational parameters were updated simultaneously. To address this, we employed a layered optimization strategy in which the first layer was optimized independently, followed by the first two layers, and so on up to kk layers. In the multilayer setting, we observed that zero initialization of the parameters was more reliable than the standard CCSD initialization for the non-generalized excitations; therefore, all-zeros initialization was used for the final results. The ADAPT-VQE operator pool we used is the set of UCCSD operators described above. For each hydrogen-chain geometry, the VQE optimization was performed independently so that every point on the curve is an independent state-preparation task.

The LUCJ ansatz was initialized using CCSD amplitudes, and the interactions were constrained to nearest neighbors on a square lattice topology (Eq. 7 of the main text). Although the double factorization of the T2T_{2} operators in Eq. 8 of the main text can approximate UCCSD reasonably well, imposing locality constraints on the interactions can significantly degrade the quality of the approximation. For this reason, we enabled compressed double factorization and mitigated Trotter errors by regularizing the norm of the diagonal Coulomb matrix [54, 85].

For the HVA, we employed a simple all-ones initialization of the variational parameters. The Hamiltonian was partitioned into commuting groups following the default implementation in Qiskit [37], without attempting to optimize for minimal sets of commuting terms.

In Sec. 4.3 of the main text, we explore optimizing circuits initialized to a UHF reference |ΨUHF⟩\lvert\Psi_{\mathrm{UHF}}\rangle. Rather than modifying the circuit structure, we implement UHF initialization through an orbital-basis transformation of the one- and two-electron integrals in Eq. 1 of the main text. Concretely, we obtain spin-dependent UHF MO coefficient matrices CαC^{\alpha} and CβC^{\beta} from the SCF calculation and form the corresponding change-of-basis matrices from the RHF MO basis to the UHF MO basis. Using these matrices, we rotate the one- and two-body integrals Tp​qT_{pq} and Vp​q​r​sV_{pqrs} into the UHF orbital basis. With the Hamiltonian expressed in this rotated basis, the standard occupation-state preparation circuit that would initialize |ΨRHF⟩\lvert\Psi_{\mathrm{RHF}}\rangle in the RHF basis instead initializes |ΨUHF⟩\lvert\Psi_{\mathrm{UHF}}\rangle in the UHF basis, and all VQE optimization is carried out with respect to this rotated Hamiltonian. This approach is computationally efficient, as the orbital rotation is performed entirely at the classical integral level and does not introduce any additional quantum circuit depth.

Once our circuits were optimized and the final statevector was obtained, we converted it into an MSD trial of the form given in Eq. 13 of the main text. This was done by masking all non–particle-number-conserving amplitudes as well as any particle-number-conserving amplitudes whose magnitudes were below double-precision threshold. We then performed ph-AFQMC using this trial state with the ipie package [58]. The initial walker states were chosen to be the RHF determinant. In combination with a spin-symmetric Hamiltonian, this ensures that the walker ensemble remains within the spin-restricted manifold throughout the imaginary-time projection, such that ⟨S^2⟩=0\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle=0, even when the trial wave function itself contains spin contamination. In the rare case that the trial state is orthogonal to the RHF determinant, the walkers are instead initialized from the determinant with the largest coefficient in the MSD expansion of the trial.

The molecular test set of Section 5 of the main text were treated with the following specifics. Geometries are the experimental equilibrium structures tabulated in the NIST Computational Chemistry Comparison and Benchmark Database [40], and all calculations use the STO-6G basis. Every molecule is treated in the full minimal-basis space except C2H2, for which the two carbon 1​s1s orbitals are frozen and the circuit spans a CAS(10e,10o) constructed with CASCI in the RHF orbital basis, so that the active integrals are an exact frozen-core reduction of the full-space ones and the trial embeds consistently in the full-space ph-AFQMC Hamiltonian. As for the hydrogen chains, UCCSD and LUCJ were initialized from unrestricted CCSD amplitudes and UpCCGSD, HVA and ADAPT-UCCSD from zero or all-ones parameters. The repetition count kk of each multilayer ansatz was chosen per molecule so that its parameter count approximately matches that of UCCSD for that molecule, which is why kk varies across the set (Table 3).

For the hydrogen chains, each trial was obtained from a single optimization using the deterministic initialization described above; the multi-start protocol was introduced for the molecular test set, where initialization sensitivity was more pronounced, particularly for UpCCGSD, HVA, and multilayer LUCJ. For these cases, we optimized from multiple starting points: in addition to the deterministic warm start, we performed restarts in which each initial parameter was perturbed by Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ=0.05\sigma=0.05, using independent random seeds. Where multiple optimizations of the same molecule and ansatz were available, the one reaching the lowest variational energy was retained as the trial wave function, and it is that trial whose properties are reported in Table 3. We note that this restart procedure does not remove the underlying difficulty: for UpCCGSD in particular, independent optimizations from equally reasonable starting points can converge to distinct local minima with substantially different variational energies and, consequently, different projected energies. This is discussed further in Section 6 of the main text.

All AFQMC simulations were run on Perlmutter CPU nodes equipped with AMD EPYC 7763 processors, with the population of single-SD walkers parallelized across many CPU threads. We used a population of 1024 walkers and the total imaginary projection time used for the quantum trial wave functions was τ=40​EHa−1\tau=40E_{\text{Ha}}^{-1}, which we found was approximately the projection time to achieve within ∼1​mHa\sim 1\,\mathrm{mHa} statistical error bars for all ansatzes, molecules, and geometries, with a few exceptions in which case we increase to τ=80​EHa−1\tau=80E_{\text{Ha}}^{-1}. For the classical benchmarks using single-determinant RHF and UHF trial wave functions, a longer imaginary-time projection was required to achieve statistical error bars below 1 mHa. Accordingly, we employed a projection time of τ=200​EHa−1\tau=200\,E_{\text{Ha}}^{-1} for these calculations. In all AFQMC simulations, the initial portion of the imaginary-time evolution was treated as equilibration (burn-in). Specifically, the first 25% of the total projection time was discarded to ensure that the walker population had equilibrated and lost memory of the initial determinant before measurements were accumulated. Additionally, after every five propagation steps of Δ​τ=0.01​EHa−1\Delta\tau=0.01\,E_{\text{Ha}}^{-1}, each walker is reorthonormalized to maintain numerical stability. At the same frequency, population control is performed: walkers with larger weights are stochastically cloned, while those with smaller weights are removed, in order to stabilize the ensemble and reduce statistical variance.

After imaginary-time evolution, we accounted for the autocorrelation present in successive local-energy measurements. To obtain statistically reliable error estimates, we performed reblocking analysis, in which correlated samples are grouped into blocks whose size is increased until the block-averaged energies become uncorrelated. The resulting integrated autocorrelation time was then used to compute accurate error bars for all reported AFQMC energies.

Appendix B ph-AFQMC: Algorithmic Details

To perform imaginary-time propagation of the Hamiltonian in Eq. 1 of the main text, the two-body term must be recast in terms of one-body operators through the introduction of auxiliary fields. This can be done by first choosing a small imaginary-time step Δ​τ>0\Delta\tau>0 and applying the Trotter–Suzuki approximation:

e−Δ​τ​H^≈e−Δ​τ​H^1​e−Δ​τ​H^2+𝒪⁡(Δ​τ2).e^{-\Delta\tau\hat{H}}\approx e^{-\Delta\tau\hat{H}_{1}}e^{-\Delta\tau\hat{H}_{2}}+\mathcal{O}(\Delta\tau^{2}). (17)

Next, we factorize the two-electron integrals Vp​q​r​sV_{pqrs} using the Cholesky decomposition:

Vp​q​r​s=12​∑γ=1NauxLp​rγ​Lq​sγ,V_{pqrs}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\gamma=1}^{N_{\mathrm{aux}}}L^{\gamma}_{pr}L^{\gamma}_{qs}, (18)

which allows the two-body part of the Hamiltonian, H^2\hat{H}_{2}, to be written as a sum of squares of one-body operators v^γ\hat{v}_{\gamma}:

H^2=12​∑γ=1Nauxλγ​v^γ2.\hat{H}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\gamma=1}^{N_{\mathrm{aux}}}\lambda_{\gamma}\hat{v}_{\gamma}^{2}. (19)

Having expressed H^2\hat{H}_{2} in this quadratic form, we can apply the Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation to express its imaginary-time propagator as an integral over NauxN_{\mathrm{aux}} auxiliary fields:

e−Δ​τ​H^2=∏γ=1Naux∫dxγe−xγ2/2exγ​−Δ​τ​λγ​v^γ+𝒪(Δτ2).e^{-\Delta\tau\hat{H}_{2}}=\prod_{\gamma=1}^{N_{\mathrm{aux}}}\int dx_{\gamma}\,e^{-x_{\gamma}^{2}/2}e^{x_{\gamma}\sqrt{-\Delta\tau\,\lambda_{\gamma}}\,\hat{v}_{\gamma}}+\mathcal{O}(\Delta\tau^{2}). (20)

By incorporating the one-body term H^1\hat{H}_{1} and collecting constants, the full imaginary-time propagator of the Hamiltonian can be written in the compact form of Eq. 14 of the main text.

The phaseless approximation incorporates importance sampling to constrain the walkers to remain within the phase sector defined by the trial wave function |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}}. This constraint suppresses destructive phase cancellations arising from random fluctuations, thereby stabilizing the simulation at the cost of a controllable bias, the accuracy of which is determined by the quality of |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}}.

With importance sampling, we assign a manipulable weight, wk​(τ)w_{k}(\tau), to each walker such that the weighted average over all NWN_{W} walkers represents the many-body wave function:

|Ψ⁡(τ)⟩=∑k=1NWwk​(τ)​|ϕk​(τ)⟩⟨ΨT|ϕk​(τ)⟩.|\Psi(\tau)\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^{N_{W}}w_{k}(\tau)\,\frac{|\phi_{k}(\tau)\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi_{k}(\tau)\rangle}. (21)

To constrain the propagation of the walkers toward the trial state |ΨT⟩|\Psi_{T}\rangle, we modify the distribution p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}) of auxiliary fields to minimize fluctuations in the overlap ratio ⟨ΨT|ϕk′⟩/⟨ΨT|ϕk⟩\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi_{k}^{\prime}\rangle/\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi_{k}\rangle, where |ϕk′⟩=B^​(𝐱)​|ϕk⟩|\phi_{k}^{\prime}\rangle=\hat{B}(\mathbf{x})|\phi_{k}\rangle. The optimal shift of the auxiliary fields, known as the force bias, is:

𝐱¯k​(τ)=−Δ​τ​⟨ΨT​|𝐯^|​ϕk​(τ)⟩⟨ΨT|ϕk​(τ)⟩,\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k}(\tau)=-\sqrt{\Delta\tau}\,\frac{\langle\Psi_{T}|\hat{\mathbf{v}}|\phi_{k}(\tau)\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi_{k}(\tau)\rangle}, (22)

where 𝐯^\hat{\mathbf{v}} denotes the collection of one-body operators introduced in Eq. 19.

We then use a shifted distribution p⁡(𝐱−𝐱¯k)p(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k}) to propagate the walkers. Under this shift, the overlap ratio becomes:

Ok​(τ)=⟨ΨT|B^​(𝐱k−𝐱¯k)|ϕk​(τ)⟩⟨ΨT|ϕk​(τ)⟩.O_{k}(\tau)=\frac{\langle\Psi_{T}|\hat{B}(\mathbf{x}_{k}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k})|\phi_{k}(\tau)\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{T}|\phi_{k}(\tau)\rangle}. (23)

To assign larger weights to walkers with larger overlaps, we define the importance function:

I⁡(𝐱k,𝐱¯k,τ)=Ok​(τ)​exp⁡(𝐱k⋅𝐱¯k−12​𝐱¯k⋅𝐱¯k),I(\mathbf{x}_{k},\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k},\tau)=O_{k}(\tau)\,\exp\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{k}\!\cdot\!\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k}-\tfrac{1}{2}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k}\!\cdot\!\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k}\right), (24)

where the exponential prefactor arises from the force-bias shift.

The phaseless approximation projects each walker’s complex weight onto the real axis by modifying the importance function:

Iph​(𝐱k,𝐱¯k,τ)=|I⁡(𝐱k,𝐱¯k,τ)|​max⁡[0,cos⁡(θk​(τ))],I_{\mathrm{ph}}(\mathbf{x}_{k},\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k},\tau)=\big|I(\mathbf{x}_{k},\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k},\tau)\big|\,\max\!\left[0,\cos\!\big(\theta_{k}(\tau)\big)\right], (25)

where the phase angle that is determined by the trial state is:

θk​(τ)=arg⁡(Ok​(τ)).\theta_{k}(\tau)=\arg\!\big(O_{k}(\tau)\big). (26)

With this constraint, the walker weights and SDs are updated as:

wk​(τ+Δ​τ)\displaystyle w_{k}(\tau+\Delta\tau) =Iph​(𝐱k,𝐱¯k,τ)​wk​(τ),\displaystyle=I_{\mathrm{ph}}(\mathbf{x}_{k},\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k},\tau)\,w_{k}(\tau), (27)
|ϕk​(τ+Δ​τ)⟩\displaystyle|\phi_{k}(\tau+\Delta\tau)\rangle =B^​(𝐱k−𝐱¯k)​|ϕk​(τ)⟩.\displaystyle=\hat{B}(\mathbf{x}_{k}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k})\,|\phi_{k}(\tau)\rangle. (28)

To summarize the importance sampling procedure, at each time step and for each walker, the auxiliary-field distribution p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}) is shifted by the optimal force bias 𝐱¯k\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k}, while the importance function Ip​hI_{ph} reweights the walkers to minimize fluctuations in overlap ratio, thereby steering the population toward physically meaningful regions of SD space guided by |ΨT⟩\ket{\Psi_{T}} [73, 58].

Appendix C Tabulated Benchmark Results

Table 2 provides a detailed summary of the VQE and ph-AFQMC results for H8 and H10 at multiple bond lengths spanning weakly to strongly correlated regimes. For each ansatz, we report the number of variational parameters, the number of optimization iterations required for convergence, the VQE correlation energy and fidelity with respect to FCI, the ⟨S2^⟩\langle\hat{S^{2}}\rangle of the trial states, the singlet-projected fidelity FS=0F_{S=0} of Eq. 16 of the main text, the number of determinants in the multideterminant expansion obtained from the optimized statevector, and the corresponding AFQMC correlation energy with statistical uncertainties. The H10 results reported here are a subset of the results used to construct the potential energy surface and fidelity comparisons shown in Figs. 1 and 2 of the main text. We include results for H8 to demonstrate that the trends observed for H10 persist across other hydrogen chains.

Table 5 reports a direct comparison of our AFQMC(UHF) total energies for H10 with the Simons Foundation hydrogen chain benchmark data. The agreement is within statistical uncertainty at all reported geometries, validating both our AFQMC implementation and our UHF-based trial protocol.

Appendix D Ansatz Depth Study

Fig. 8 presents a systematic study of ansatz expressivity for H8 at three representative bond lengths, with both the VQE and the ph-AFQMC errors shown as functions of the number of variational parameters. Successive points along each curve correspond to increasing repetition count kk, and the range shown extends to roughly 1.5 times the parameter count of UCCSD for H8 (360, Table 2), which brackets the parameter-matched depths used for the comparisons in the main text. Within this range, LUCJ and HVA both improve systematically in the variational and in the projected energy as parameters are added, at every bond length, with the largest gains occurring in the intermediate and strongly correlated regimes. At matched parameter counts, HVA yields the more accurate projected energy at all three bond lengths, and at R=1.8R=1.8 Å it does so despite a higher variational energy than LUCJ, suggesting that HVA circuits provide a phase structure better suited to the phaseless constraint for these systems than their variational energy alone would indicate. This is consistent with the H10 results in the main text. In contrast, UpCCGSD plateaus earliest in both the variational and the projected energy, and additional layers do not yield further improvement. These results reinforce the central theme of this work, with an important qualification: adequate expressivity, achieved either through increased depth or adaptive construction, improves phaseless performance, but only insofar as the optimization can realize it, and the optimal balance between parameter count and optimization tractability is ansatz dependent.

Appendix E Optimization Cost and Circuit Resources

Table 6 reports the cost of preparing each trial wave function for the two most strongly correlated systems in the benchmark set, H10 at R=2.0R=2.0 Å and C2, along two independent axes: the classical cost of carrying out the variational optimization, and the size of the circuit that would have to be executed on hardware. The two do not track each other, and neither tracks accuracy.

The first is the measured wall-clock cost of the optimization on GPU nodes, expressed relative to the cheapest ansatz for that system so that the comparison is not tied to a particular machine or node count. HVA is the most expensive optimization for C2 by more than an order of magnitude, and among the most expensive for H10, while being one of the more inaccurate ansatz on both systems (Table 3). The cost follows from the structure of the ansatz: the number of variational parameters per HVA layer is the number of mutually commuting groups of the qubit Hamiltonian, 120 for H10 and 77 for C2, which grows quickly with the complexity of the electronic structure, and every one of those parameters requires its own gradient evaluation at every optimization step. ADAPT-UCCSD is expensive for the opposite reason: it produces the shortest circuit of the UCC family, but the operator-pool gradient screening performed before each operator is appended dominates its total cost. The low optimization cost of UCCSD relative to the other ansatzes should also be understood in light of its initialization. Its variational parameters are initialized from amplitudes obtained from an unrestricted CCSD calculation, providing a physically informed starting point that substantially reduces the number of optimization iterations required compared with an uninformed initialization. Although this initialization is most effective in the weakly correlated regime, it remains a useful starting point for the strongly correlated systems considered here.

The second is an estimate of the two-qubit gate count of the corresponding circuit. These counts are structural rather than compiled. All simulations in this work were performed with GPU state-vector simulators, so the circuits are never transpiled to a hardware gate set and no compiled counts exist for them. For the ansatzes built from Pauli exponentials, UCCSD, ADAPT-UCCSD, UpCCGSD and HVA, each factor e−i​θ​Pe^{-i\theta P} acting on a Pauli word PP of weight ww is counted in the textbook CNOT-ladder form: a staircase of w−1w-1 cnots, one single-qubit rotation, and the reversed staircase, for 2​(w−1)2(w-1) two-qubit gates. The counts are summed over every Pauli word of every generator in the circuit and multiplied by the number of layers. LUCJ is counted directly from its own gate structure, as Givens-rotation networks for the orbital rotations together with the paired X​X+Y​YXX+YY interactions and the diagonal-Coulomb Z​ZZZ phases. No circuit optimization of any kind is applied: adjacent cnots between neighboring Pauli terms are not cancelled, JW strings are not shared between terms, and all-to-all qubit connectivity is assumed so that no swap overhead is incurred. A real compiler targeting a specific device would reduce these numbers substantially for the UCC-type circuits, while restricted connectivity would increase them. They should therefore be read as an order-of-magnitude proxy for relative circuit depth across ansatzes, not as a resource requirement for any particular device.

Read that way, the gate counts separate the ansatzes far more sharply than the optimization cost does, and they do not order them the same way. LUCJ yields substantially shallower circuits than the other ansatzes considered, by construction: its two-body correlations are restricted to a fixed interaction pattern rather than to the full set of excitations. HVA is the deepest by a wide margin, roughly 5×5\times UCCSD for H10 and 4×4\times for C2, because it exponentiates every Pauli term of the JW Hamiltonian once per layer, including the long parity strings, which reach weight 20 on 20 qubits. The combination of LUCJ’s shallow circuits with its accuracy at these geometries (Figures 1(b) and 6 of the main text) is the most favorable trade-off in the set.

Appendix F Concordance Analysis with Statistical Uncertainty

The per-system concordances in Figure 7 of the main text treat each ph-AFQMC energy as exact. To account for statistical uncertainty in the projected energies, we also compute concordance pooled across systems, restricting the analysis to trial pairs (A,B)(A,B) from the same system whose absolute ph-AFQMC errors are resolvable according to ||Δ​EA|−|Δ​EB||>2​σA2+σB2\big||\Delta E_{A}|-|\Delta E_{B}|\big|>2\sqrt{\sigma_{A}^{2}+\sigma_{B}^{2}}, where Δ​Ei=EAFQMC,i−EFCI\Delta E_{i}=E_{\mathrm{AFQMC},i}-E_{\mathrm{FCI}} is the ph-AFQMC energy error for trial ii and σi\sigma_{i} is its statistical uncertainty. Because trial pairs within a system are not independent, we estimate 95% confidence intervals using a cluster bootstrap over systems. Specifically, we generate 4000 resampled datasets by randomly selecting whole systems with replacement and recompute the concordance for each dataset. The resulting variation in concordance provides an estimate of its statistical uncertainty.

As shown in Figure 9, the ordering by variational energy, fidelity FF, and spin-projected fidelity FS=0F_{S=0} agrees with the ordering by absolute ph-AFQMC error for 75%, 86%, and 95% of the resolvable pairs, respectively. To compare the diagnostics directly, their differences in concordance are computed within each of the same bootstrap resamples. The paired differences are +10+10% (95% CI: +2+2 to +21+21%) for FF relative to variational energy, +19+19% (+8+8 to +31+31%) for FS=0F_{S=0} relative to variational energy, and +8+8% (+3+3 to +15+15%) for FS=0F_{S=0} relative to FF. The same ordering of the three diagnostics is obtained for resolvability thresholds ranging from 0​σ0\sigma to 3​σ3\sigma.
